About ClientFlow

We built this for our own clients first. Then we opened the doors.

ClientFlow didn't start as software. It started as an agency running marketing for gyms and wellness clinics around Ireland. We built their websites, filled their classes, chased their leads and watched their bills — and we kept hitting the same wall: the tools they paid for were expensive, splintered across five vendors, quick to hike prices, and none of them could give a client a real website. So we built our own platform to run our clients' businesses properly. It worked. Owners kept asking if they could just have the thing we'd built. Eventually we said yes, and productised it. That's ClientFlow.

Why flat pricing

€200, flat, forever-honest — on purpose.

We've sat on the customer side of the add-on trap. We've watched "starter" prices quietly become €400 bills, and month-to-month promises turn into contracts. So flat, published, month-to-month pricing isn't a marketing angle for us — it's a reaction to everything we hated. One price. Everything on. Cancel whenever. If we ever have to raise it, you'll opt in, not get ambushed.

Published on this page
€200

Flat, per month — never "starting at," never "contact sales."

Built in Ireland

Made in Ireland 🇮🇪, for Ireland and the UK.

We're built and based in Ireland, and we understand the market our customers work in — VAT, local SEO, the way a Clonmel gym or a Cork clinic actually wins customers. When you call support, you're talking to the people who built the product, not a queue three time zones away.

This policy explains how Christopher Walshe ("ClientFlow", "we", "us") collects, uses and protects personal data. Christopher Walshe

Data we collect

Account and business data. When you sign up, book a demo or contact us, we collect your name, business name, email, phone number, business type, billing details and login credentials.

Member and client data (processed on behalf of gyms and clinics). When you use ClientFlow to run your business, you upload personal data about your members and clients — names, contact details, bookings, attendance, memberships, packages, payment records and notes. We process this only to provide the service to you, under your instructions.

Payment data. Card and payment details are collected and processed by our payment processor (see Processors we use). We do not store full card numbers on our own systems.

Usage and analytics data. With your consent where required, we collect analytics about how our website and platform are used — pages viewed, device and browser type, and general location derived from IP. Non-essential analytics run only after you consent via our cookie banner.

Cookies. We use strictly necessary cookies to keep you logged in and secure, and — with consent — analytics cookies. See Cookies below.

Communications. If you connect an email inbox (e.g. Gmail) or message clients through the platform, we process the content of those communications to deliver the messaging features you've enabled.

Lawful bases

We rely on the following GDPR lawful bases:

  • Contract — to provide the platform, manage your subscription and support you.
  • Legitimate interests — to secure our systems, prevent fraud, and improve the product, balanced against your rights.
  • Consent — for non-essential analytics cookies and certain marketing communications. You can withdraw consent at any time.
  • Legal obligation — to meet accounting, tax and other legal requirements.

For member and client data you upload, your lawful basis as controller is your responsibility; we process it under our data processing terms with you.

Processors we use

We share personal data only with vetted sub-processors who help us run the service. Current processors include:

  • Railway (hosting, EU-West region) — application and database hosting.
  • Anthropic (AI processing) — powers AI marketing and assistant features. Content sent for AI processing is used to generate your output and is not used to train models under our terms.
  • Resend (email delivery) — sending transactional and marketing email.
  • Google / Gmail (where you connect it) — to provide two-way email inbox features you enable.
  • Payment processor — CreatePay / Cardstream — to process card payments securely.

We put appropriate data processing agreements and safeguards in place with each. Where any transfer outside the EEA occurs, we rely on adequacy decisions or Standard Contractual Clauses.

Google user data (Limited Use)

When you connect a Google account — for example, to use the two-way email inbox — ClientFlow requests access to your Gmail using Google’s restricted gmail.modify scope, so you can read, label, send and organise email from inside the platform. We access this data only to provide those features to you, and only while your Google account stays connected.

ClientFlow’s use and transfer to any other app of information received from Google APIs will adhere to the Google API Services User Data Policy, including the Limited Use requirements.

Specifically, ClientFlow does not:

  • use your Google user data for serving advertising;
  • transfer or sell your Google user data, except as necessary to provide or improve the feature you connected it for, to comply with applicable law, or in connection with a merger or acquisition with notice to you;
  • allow humans to read your Google user data, unless you give explicit consent for specific messages, it is necessary for security (such as investigating abuse), it is required by law, or the data has been aggregated and anonymised; or
  • use your Google user data to train generalised or non-personalised AI or machine-learning models.

You can disconnect Google at any time in Settings → Email. When you disconnect, we delete the stored Google authorisation tokens for that account; while connected, those tokens are held encrypted at rest. To request deletion of email already synced into your ClientFlow account, email chris@clientflow.ie.

You also have the right to lodge a complaint with the Irish Data Protection Commission (dataprotection.ie) or your local supervisory authority.

If you are a member or client of a gym or clinic that uses ClientFlow, please direct requests to that business first — they are the controller of your data. We will assist them in responding.

To exercise your rights against us as controller, contact chris@clientflow.ie.

posts.title: How Much Does Gym Management Software Really Cost in Ireland? (2026 Breakdown)
posts.content:
# How much does gym management software really cost in Ireland? (2026 breakdown)

Ask a gym software salesperson what their platform costs and you'll get a clean number. Ask an owner who's run it for a year what they actually paid, and you'll get a very different one. The gap between the two rarely shows up as one shock invoice — it shows up as five or six small ones, stacked quietly across your card statement every month.

We went through the pricing and add-on structure of 37 gym and studio platforms in July 2026 to see what Irish gym, studio and clinic owners are really signing up for. Here's the honest version.

## The advertised price is never the whole price

The pattern is consistent across almost every platform on the market: the headline tier gets you in the door, but it rarely includes what a real, growing gym actually needs — a branded app with your name on it, a workable payment rate, more than one staff login, and (in 25 of the 37 platforms we reviewed) any website at all.

Fourteen of the 37 don't publish pricing anywhere on their site — you only find the real number after a sales call, by which point you've usually had a demo, filled in a form, and started picturing your gym on the new system. That's not an accident. It's a sales process built around the fact that a published number invites comparison, and an unpublished one doesn't.

## What the big platforms actually cost, add-on by add-on

Figures below are from our July 2026 research. Verified figures are marked as such; everything else is our own estimate built from published add-on pricing, and flagged clearly.

### Mindbody

- **Starter plan: $79 / €99 a month (verified).** This is the studio-management layer only — scheduling, basic client records.
- **Branded app: not included.** Estimated at $249–299 a month (researched estimate) if you want your own app in the App Store and Play Store, rather than clients booking you through Mindbody's own consumer app alongside every other studio in town.
- **Payments: 2.75–3.6%**, plus a 20% marketplace commission on new clients who found you via the Mindbody marketplace, capped at $30 per client.
- **Real tiers for a working studio:** contact-sales pricing, estimated at $259–699 a month once you need the features a full gym actually uses.
- Mindbody holds a 3.7 rating on G2 — and, worth knowing before you sign anything, 89% negative reviews specifically about the cancellation experience.

### Glofox

- **Essential plan: $99 a month (verified).**
- Branded app and proper CRM functionality are add-ons *below* the Elite tier — meaning things most owners assume are "just part of the software" start out as paid extras.
- Higher tiers are opaque, with no published pricing.
- **No website product at all.** Glofox is a booking widget you embed on a site you build and host somewhere else, at your own cost.
- Trustpilot rating: 3.5. Some customers have reported price increases as steep as 70% after their first contract term — worth asking about directly before you sign.

### TeamUp and Gymdesk

Both are often positioned as the "affordable" option — until you look at what's missing from the base price.

- **TeamUp's** branded app is a $99-a-month add-on. Feature-parity total cost of ownership (core platform + app + a workable payment setup) lands around **$320–350 a month** (researched estimate).
- **Gymdesk's** branded app add-on runs about **$100 a month**, with a feature-parity total around **$300 a month** (researched estimate).

### LegitFit — the Irish option, with its own catch

LegitFit is Cork-founded and well-regarded — a 4.9 on Capterra, which is a genuinely strong number. But two things are worth knowing:

- Its pricing was historically published at €79 / €129 / €249 tiers, but as of our July 2026 research it's now **quote-gated** — you talk to sales to get a number.
- Like Glofox, it has **no website product**. You're building and hosting your site elsewhere, and its branded app and AI features sit behind paid add-ons on top of the base plan.

### The heaviest hitters once you add it all up

Matching core CRM, a branded app, and a workable payment rate, our researched feature-parity totals land around **$510–580 a month for Mindbody** and **$559 a month for PushPress** — both a long way from the number on the homepage.

## The per-member creep nobody warns you about

Beyond the headline add-ons, watch for the costs that only appear as you grow:

- **Member or booking count tiers.** Cross a threshold and you're bumped to the next pricing band — growth gets taxed.
- **Extra staff logins.** Most base tiers include one or two; a real team needs more.
- **SMS and email overages.** A bundled allowance runs out fast during a promotion or a busy sign-up month.
- **Multi-location surcharges.** Opening a second site rarely means the second site is free.
- **Payment processing stacked with marketplace commission** — two separate charges on the same transaction, from the same provider.

## Payment processing: the take-rate hiding in your bank statement

This is the line owners check least and lose the most on. ## Build your own total-cost worksheet

Don't take the homepage number at face value. Add up what you'd actually need:

| Cost line | What to check | Typical range (researched, July 2026) |
|---|---|---|
| Core CRM / scheduling | Base fee at the tier you'd actually use | $79–$249+/month |
| Branded mobile app | Usually a separate add-on | $99–$349/month |
| Payment processing | % rate + marketplace commission | 1.3–3.6% + 0–20% |
| Website | Often not included at all | €0 (DIY) to €3,000+ build, plus hosting |
| Extra staff seats | Per-login fees above a base allowance | Varies by platform |
| SMS / email marketing | Per-send fees after a bundled allowance | Varies by platform |

Run your own numbers through that table for the plan you'd actually need — not the plan on the homepage — and most Irish studios we've reviewed land somewhere between €300 and €580 a month, before they've spent a cent on marketing.

posts.content:
# Gym website ideas that actually bring in members

Most gym websites are digital business cards, not sales tools. Someone finds you on Google, lands on a slow page with stock photography and a "Contact Us" button, and leaves before they ever see your timetable. Fixing that is rarely about a redesign — it's about understanding what a gym website actually needs to do, and building around that.

## Why "a widget on a template site" underperforms

Here's the setup a lot of Irish gyms end up with without quite choosing it: the gym management platform handles bookings and payments in the back office, and the "website" is a Wix, Squarespace or Webador page with the platform's booking widget embedded as an iframe. Two different companies, built separately, bolted together.

It's worth knowing this isn't a fringe case — in our July 2026 review of 37 gym and studio platforms, **25 had no website product of their own at all**. Widgets-on-a-template-site isn't a shortcut some gyms take; for two-thirds of the market, it's the only option on offer.

The consequences are consistent:

- **Slow load times.** Iframes are heavy, and a widget loading on top of an already-built page adds a second, visible delay.
- **A visual seam.** The moment a visitor clicks "book," the design changes — different fonts, different colours, sometimes a different logo entirely.
- **No SEO value from the booking flow.** Widget content usually isn't part of your crawlable page, so the class names, descriptions and search terms inside it do nothing for your ranking.
- **Broken mobile styling.** Widgets are built to fit inside any host site, which usually means they fit none of them particularly well.

## Local SEO for gyms — the fundamentals that actually move the needle

### Google Business Profile is your highest-leverage asset

Keep hours, categories and photos current, collect reviews as a routine part of your member experience, and post updates regularly. For most local searches — "gym near me," "PT in [town]" — this shows up before your website does.

### NAP consistency

Your Name, Address and Phone number need to match exactly across your website, your Google Business Profile, and every directory you're listed in. Inconsistency here — "St." versus "Street," an old phone number on one listing — quietly costs local ranking without ever throwing an obvious error.

### Location-specific landing pages

Don't rely on one homepage to rank for every area you serve. A page built for "personal training in Clonmel" is worth more, for that search, than a homepage that mentions Clonmel once in the footer. This matters most for multi-location studios or clinics drawing from a wider catchment — a Tipperary clinic pulling clients from Cahir, Cashel and Carrick-on-Suir benefits from a page for each, not one page trying to cover all three.

### Page speed and mobile-first

Most "gym near me" searches happen on a phone, standing still, deciding in the next ten seconds whether to call or move to the next result. A widget-heavy site that takes six seconds to load has usually lost that visitor before the timetable even renders.

### Reviews and local backlinks

Genuine local signals compound: sponsoring a local club or event, getting covered by local press, and being listed properly in local directories all build the kind of backlink profile that a national competitor with a bigger ad budget can't easily out-rank.

## Content ideas that compound your local SEO over time

A blog only helps your ranking if it targets searches real people in your area are actually making. Topics that consistently work for gyms and clinics:

- **"[Class type] for beginners in [Town]"** guides — captures people who are interested but nervous about walking in cold.
- **Local event recaps** — a charity run you sponsored, a community class, a local sports team you support. These attract local links as well as local search traffic.
- **Seasonal content timed to real behaviour** — "getting back into training after Christmas" performs every January in the Irish market for a reason.
- **Buyer-question posts** that answer what people are already typing into Google — "what does a personal trainer cost in Ireland," "how does HBOT work," "what to expect at your first session."
- **Real, consented client result stories** — the single highest-converting content type on most gym and clinic sites, and the one most sites skip because it takes longer to produce properly.

## What a converting gym website actually needs

A practical checklist:

- **A trial offer above the fold** — not "Learn more," an actual first step: book a free class, claim a trial week.
- **Instant booking**, not "call us" or "email us." Every extra step between interest and booking loses people.
- **Real photos** of your actual space and actual members, not stock gym photography that could belong to any gym in the country.
- **A visible price, or a clear next step** if pricing genuinely needs a consultation — ambiguity here is one of the biggest silent drop-off points.
- **A timetable that works on a phone** — large tap targets, not a tiny embedded grid designed for a desktop screen.
- **Instructor bios with real names and faces** — this builds trust before anyone walks through the door.
- **A blog or content section** targeting the local searches from the SEO section above — this is also where fresh content compounds your ranking over time.
- **Fast load time**, treated as a KPI you check, not an afterthought you hope is fine.

## Sections that actually work

Some specific page elements worth building deliberately, rather than leaving to a template default:

- An **above-the-fold trial-offer banner** with one clear call to action — not three competing buttons.
- An **embedded, brand-matched timetable** that's genuinely part of the page, not a widget wearing your colours as a costume.
- A **"meet your coaches" grid** with names, faces and specialities.
- A **results section built from real, consented member stories** once you have them — this is worth waiting for rather than faking; a handful of real stories always outperforms a page of generic claims.
- A **location page per branch**, with an embedded map, local hours, and directions specific to that site.
- An **FAQ section** addressing the actual objections that stop a booking: parking, whether beginners are welcome, contract length.
- A **"what to expect at your first visit"** section — especially valuable for clinics and studios, where nerves about walking in the door are a bigger drop-off point than price.

## How to tell if your website is actually working

A handful of numbers tell you more than how it looks:

- **Booking conversion rate** — the share of visitors who actually book, not just browse. If it's stuck in the low single digits, the problem is usually friction in the booking flow, not the traffic.
- **Mobile load time** — aim under roughly 2.5 seconds. Anything slower and you're losing the phone-in-hand searches the local SEO work above is meant to win.
- **Traffic source** — know how much comes from Google Business Profile, organic search, paid, and social. If it's almost entirely paid, your organic and local SEO foundations still need work.
- **Bounce rate on your timetable or booking page specifically** — not just the homepage. This is the page where genuine interest turns into a booking or quietly disappears.

## Where ClientFlow fits

This is the gap we built ClientFlow to close. Every plan includes a real website — designed, built and hosted by us, wired directly into your booking and membership system rather than bolted on as a widget — plus an AI marketing studio to keep content and local landing pages fresh without hiring an agency to do it.

If your current site is just a booking widget bolted onto someone else's template, [see pricing](/pricing) to see what's actually included, or [book a demo](/book-a-demo) and we'll show you what a real one looks like.

posts.title: How to Switch Gym Software Without Losing Members or Payments
posts.content:
# How to switch gym software without losing members or payments

Most gym owners who hate their software don't switch. Not because the alternative isn't better — usually they know exactly which platform they'd rather be on — but because the migration itself feels like the riskier bet. Lost payment mandates. Confused members. A double-charge that turns into a refund request and a one-star review. The fear of a bad switch is often the real lock-in, more than any contract term ever was.

Done properly, switching is a managed project with a known shape. Here's the playbook.

## Why "we'll switch eventually" usually means "we'll never switch"

The risk isn't imaginary — it's just manageable. The things that actually go wrong during a bad migration are specific and predictable: member records go missing, payment authorisations don't carry over cleanly, credits or session balances get lost in translation, and nobody tells members anything until the day it happens. Every one of those is avoidable with a plan.

There's also a second, quieter reason owners stall: they assume a switch means an all-or-nothing weekend of chaos. It doesn't have to. Treated as a staged project with a fixed shape — export, overlap, communicate, cut over — it's closer to changing a payment terminal than rebuilding the business.

## How long a migration actually takes

A realistic timeline for a single-site studio or clinic looks something like this:

| Phase | Timing | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| Scoping & export | Weeks -4 to -3 | Confirm what data you can export, request the file, verify it's complete |
| Import & staff training | Week -2 | New platform populated and tested; front-desk and coaching staff trained on it |
| Overlap window | Week -1 to Week +4 | Both systems run in parallel; new one takes live bookings and payments |
| Close-out | Week +5 | Balances reconciled, old platform switched off, migration formally closed |

Multi-location businesses or larger clinics should expect the export and training phases to run longer, simply because there's more staff to train and more historical data to check.

## The migration playbook

### Step 1 — Export everything before you touch anything else

Before you sign with a new platform, confirm you can get a clean export of:

- Member and client records (contact details, DOB, emergency contacts, and — for clinics — medical or PARQ notes)
- Payment mandates and billing history, not just the token but the underlying consent record
- Class and attendance history
- Package or membership balances (credits owed, sessions remaining)
- Signed waivers and agreements
- Marketing consent status — important under GDPR for any Irish or EU business

If a platform makes this export difficult or slow, treat that as information. The easier your data is to leave with, the more it tells you about how that company thinks about lock-in.

### Step 2 — Payment mandates: the part everyone gets wrong

You generally can't copy a card number from one processor to another — PCI rules don't allow it, and no reputable platform will offer to. There are two real paths:

1. **Provider-to-provider token migration**, where it's supported. Ask both platforms directly whether this is possible for your specific processor; some same-processor migrations (Stripe to Stripe, for example) can sometimes carry tokens across, but cross-processor moves usually can't.
2. **Re-authorisation.** The member re-enters their payment details once, ideally inside the new branded app or portal so it feels like an upgrade rather than admin.

Whichever path applies, time the cutover to land on a natural billing date, not mid-cycle — a payment gap or an accidental double-charge is the single fastest way to generate support tickets and lose trust in week one.

### Step 3 — Run a 30-day overlap window

Don't flip a switch overnight. Run both systems in parallel for a defined window: the old platform stays live in a read-only or billing-only capacity while the new one takes live bookings, so nothing falls through the cracks. Reconcile the data at day 30, confirm balances match, and only then switch the old platform off.

### Step 4 — Member communications timeline

A simple four-touch timeline covers most of what members need to hear:

- **T-30 days:** what's changing, why, and — critically — what stays the same (their price, their sessions, their trainer).
- **T-14 days:** the new app, with a download link and login steps.
- **T-7 days:** a short reminder for anyone who hasn't logged in yet, with an offer of help for members who aren't confident with apps.
- **T-1 day:** a reminder that tomorrow's the day, with reassurance that bookings and credits have already carried across.
- **T+1 day:** a check-in confirming they're set up, with a named contact if anything looks off.

A short example for the T-30 message:

> "Hi [Name] — quick heads up: from [date] we're moving to a new booking app that makes it easier to book classes and manage your membership. Nothing changes about your price or your sessions — they've all carried across. Download the new app here: [link]. Questions? Just reply to this text."

And for T+1:

> "You're all set on the new system, [Name] — your membership and remaining sessions carried across exactly as they were. If anything looks off, reply here or call us on [number] and we'll sort it same day."

### Step 5 — Cut-over day checklist

- Old system switched to read-only
- New system live for bookings and payments
- Front-desk and coaching staff briefed, with a one-page FAQ ready for members who ask
- A named person owning migration support for the first week, so questions don't get lost between people

Don't skip staff training to save a few days. The people at your front desk field more migration questions in the first week than any email or text does — if they're guessing at answers, members notice.

## Questions to ask a new platform's migration team before you sign

Get these answered before you commit, not after:

- Is migration support included, or a paid add-on on top of the subscription?
- Who actually maps and imports your data — their team, or yours?
- Can they migrate payment tokens for your specific processor, or will every member need to re-authorise?
- What's a realistic timeline for a business your size, in writing?
- If something looks wrong in week one, who do you call, and how fast do they answer?

A vendor who answers all five clearly, before you've signed anything, is telling you something real about how the first month will go.

## Common mistakes that cause member drop-off during a switch

- Migrating the Friday before your busiest weekend of the month
- No overlap window — cutting the old system off the same day the new one launches
- Forcing a password reset with no instructions attached
- Staying silent until go-live day instead of building the T-30 to T+1 timeline above
- Losing package or credit balances in the export — one of the fastest ways to break trust with a member who's tracking their sessions closely

## How ClientFlow handles migration

We run migration for every studio that switches to ClientFlow, free, as part of onboarding. We map your data export, help coordinate the payment mandate cutover with your current processor, and build your 30-day overlap plan with you so members never notice a gap.

posts.content:
# The true cost of "free" gym software

"Free" is a pricing strategy, not a gift. Somebody always pays for the software that runs your gym — the only question a free or near-free platform is really asking is whether that somebody is you, your members, or your growth. Usually, once you scale past a certain size, it's the last one.

## How "free" gym software actually makes its money

Low-cost and "free" platforms in this space tend to run on one of two engines, often both at once: a **marketplace commission** on new clients, and a **payment processing margin** baked into every transaction you run.

### The marketplace commission model

Fresha is the clearest example of this in the Irish and UK market. Its published structure, as of our July 2026 research, runs:

- **Seat fees of €9.95–14.95 a month per team member**
- **Payment processing at 1.29% + €0.20 per transaction**
- **A 20% commission on new clients** who book and pay for the first time through Fresha's own marketplace — with a minimum of €5 per new client

That last line is the one that matters most. It's not a fee on your software — it's a fee on your growth. Every new client the marketplace sends you costs 20% of their first booking, indefinitely, with no cap mentioned in the published structure.

### The payment-margin model

Mindbody runs a related version of the same logic: payment processing at 2.75–3.6%, plus a 20% marketplace commission on clients sourced through its own marketplace — but capped at $30 per client. That cap matters more than it looks. A studio selling a €300 introductory package pays a full €60 under an uncapped structure, versus a $30 ceiling under a capped one. Same mechanism, very different exposure depending on what you charge.

### The two models, side by side

|  | Fresha | Mindbody |
|---|---|---|
| Seat fee | €9.95–14.95/month per team member | Included in platform fee |
| Payment processing | 1.29% + €0.20 per transaction | 2.75–3.6% |
| New-client commission | 20%, minimum €5, no published cap | 20%, capped at $30 per client |

Both figures are drawn from published rate structures as of July 2026. The detail that decides which one costs you more isn't the headline percentage — it's whether your average first-visit or first-package value sits comfortably under the cap, or well over it.

## Do the maths: what 20% commission costs at real volumes

Take a wellness clinic with an average first-visit value of €60, sourcing new clients through a marketplace at different volumes a month:

| New marketplace clients/month | Commission per client (20%, above €5 min) | Monthly commission cost |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | €12 | €120 |
| 25 | €12 | €300 |
| 50 | €12 | €600 |

Add seat fees (say three staff at roughly €12 a month average = €36) and payment processing at 1.29% + €0.20 across *all* transactions, not just marketplace-sourced ones, and the "free" platform has a real monthly cost before you've touched a paid ad.

At the 50-client volume, that's €600 a month in commission alone — on clients who, once they rebook, cost the platform nothing extra to serve, but who you already paid full price to meet. It's a tax on exactly the thing you're trying to do.

### What that looks like over a year

Run the 50-client scenario for twelve months and it's **€7,200 in commission alone**, before seat fees and payment processing are added on top. That's not a rounding error in a small business's marketing budget — for a lot of Irish studios and clinics, it's close to the annual cost of a part-time front-desk hire. Worth sitting with that comparison before you decide the commission model is the cheaper option because there's no monthly platform fee.

## When free (or near-free) is genuinely the right call

This model isn't wrong for everyone. It's a legitimate choice if:

- **You're pre-revenue or testing a concept** — a single trainer trialling group classes for the first time, with no appetite for a fixed monthly cost yet.
- **You bring 100% of your own clients.** If you never accept a client sourced through the platform's own marketplace, the commission line largely disappears — audit which model actually applies to you before assuming the worst case.
- **Your transaction volume is genuinely low.** A flat fee elsewhere isn't justified yet if you're processing a handful of bookings a month.

## When free starts taxing your growth

The maths flips once any of these become true:

- **You're running your own marketing.** Paid ads or organic content that drives a booking through the marketplace means you're paying twice for the same new client — your own spend, plus the marketplace's cut.
- **Your team grows.** Seat fees stack per person, every month, regardless of how busy any individual is.
- **You want your brand front and centre.** A marketplace listing puts you next to direct competitors in the same search results — "free" discovery cuts both ways.
- **Your average order value rises.** Higher-ticket clinic packages make an uncapped percentage commission expensive fast, as the €300-package example above shows.

## The hidden costs beyond the commission line

A few extra things worth knowing before you commit long-term to a commission-based platform:

- **No website product is bundled.** You're still paying for a site separately, same as with most paid platforms in this space.
- **Your data and client relationship sit partly inside someone else's ecosystem**, not fully under your own brand.
- **Pricing pressure.** Marketplace search results tend to reward the cheapest listing, which can quietly pull your prices down over time.

## Questions to ask before you sign a commission-based platform

Before committing, get straight answers on:

- Is the new-client commission capped, or does it scale uncapped with the value of the first booking or package?
- Does the commission apply only to genuinely new clients, or also to lapsed clients who rebook after a gap?
- What counts as "marketplace-sourced" versus a client you brought yourself through your own marketing — and how is that actually tracked and reported to you?
- Do seat fees apply per active login, or per staff member regardless of how often they use the system?
- Is there a published rate card anywhere, or does confirming the real structure require a sales call?

If a vendor can't give you a straight answer to the first two questions, assume the worst-case version of both until they can.

## What we did differently with ClientFlow

We built ClientFlow the other way round. €200 a month, flat, and every client who books through your ClientFlow website or app is 100% yours — no new-client marketplace commission, ever. Payments run roughly 40% below standard Stripe rates with zero marketplace cut on top. You know your number on the first of the month, and it doesn't move just because business is going well.
